subsection: 1. Case study of a developed economy: Ireland

notes.b: Economic activities are grouped into three sectors by what they do with raw materials or with people's needs.
points: Primary: extracting raw materials from nature, such as farming, fishing, forestry, mining, quarrying and energy extraction.
Secondary: processing raw materials or assembling components into goods, such as manufacturing, food processing and construction.
Tertiary: services, such as retail, banking, tourism, teaching, health, transport and IT.
Classifying jobs: a miner or forester is primary; a builder is secondary, because construction is secondary; a teacher, banker or tour guide is tertiary.
Some writers add a quaternary sector for research and information, but the three-sector model is used here.

notes.h: Sectoral change as an economy develops
points: As an economy develops, employment moves from primary to secondary and then to tertiary activity.
Services employ about three-quarters of Irish workers (2020s); agriculture, forestry and fishing employ about 4–5%.
Census 2022 counted a State population of about 5.1 million; the CSO Labour Force Survey (2024) recorded over 2.7 million people in employment.
In a developing economy, by contrast, primary employment is high (see the Economic Development notes).
The Control of Manufactures Acts, 1932 and 1934, restricted foreign ownership of Irish firms.
High tariffs protected small Irish firms serving the home market, so they had little pressure to become efficient or to export.
The 1950s brought high unemployment and heavy emigration.

notes.h: Free trade and foreign investment, 1949 to 1973
points: The Industrial Development Authority (IDA) was set up in 1949 to attract industry.
Export Profits Tax Relief, 1956, removed tax on profits from exports.

T.K. Whitaker's Economic Development and the First Programme for Economic Expansion (1958) set the policy of free trade, foreign investment and export-led growth, carried out under Seán Lemass as Taoiseach from 1959.
The Anglo-Irish Free Trade Agreement (1965) reduced trade barriers with Britain.
Ireland joined the EEC on 1 January 1973, together with the UK and Denmark.

notes.h: Education and a growing skilled workforce
points: Free second-level education was announced in 1966 by Donogh O'Malley and introduced in 1967.
A better-educated workforce made Ireland attractive to firms that needed skilled labour in the decades that followed.
The IDA became an independent agency under the Industrial Development Act 1969.

notes.h: Single Market, euro and corporation tax
points: The EU Single Market began in 1993, giving Irish firms and foreign investors access to the wider EU market.
The euro was adopted in 1999, with notes and coins introduced in 2002.
Corporation tax on trading profits was 12.5% from 2003.
From 2024 very large multinational groups (global turnover over €750 million) pay a 15% minimum rate under the OECD agreement.
Rapid growth from the mid-1990s to 2007 was driven first by exports and foreign direct investment, especially from US technology and pharmaceutical firms.
A property and construction boom added to growth later in the period.
Unemployment fell to about 4–5% by the mid-2000s.
Net immigration replaced emigration, with large inflows from the new EU states after the 2004 enlargement.
The property bubble burst in 2007–2008, leaving banks with large bad loans secured on property.
On 30 September 2008 the government guaranteed Irish bank liabilities.
Anglo Irish Bank was nationalised in January 2009.
The National Asset Management Agency (NAMA), set up in 2009, took over property loans from the banks.

notes.h: EU–IMF programme and public debt, 2010 to 2013
points: An EU–IMF programme was agreed in November 2010, providing €67.5 billion in external loans.
Ireland left the programme in December 2013.
Unemployment peaked at about 16% in early 2012; net emigration resumed from 2009 to 2014.
Government debt peaked at about 120% of GDP in 2012: the state borrowed to rescue the banks while its tax base collapsed with the economy.
Unemployment was about 4–5% in 2023–2024, near full employment.
Budget surpluses in the 2020s came largely from corporation tax paid by a small number of large multinationals, so public finances depend on them.
Employed people pay income tax, and their spending pays VAT, so tax revenue rises.
Welfare spending falls because fewer people need unemployment payments.
Consumer spending by employed people supports jobs in other sectors.
Less emigration keeps skilled people in the economy.
Government revenue can pay for investment in infrastructure and services.
In 2015 Irish GDP grew by about 26% after multinationals moved intellectual property assets to Ireland; the effect was nicknamed 'leprechaun economics'.
Because GDP is inflated by these profits, the CSO introduced modified gross national income (GNI*) in 2017 to strip out their effects.
The Census of Agriculture 2020 counted about 135,000 farms, averaging about 33 hectares.
Grass grows for most of the year because winters are mild and rain is reliable, so grass-based livestock farming dominates.
Pastoral farming is livestock farming: beef and dairy cattle, sheep and pigs. The national cattle herd is about 7 million (2020s).
Arable (tillage) farming grows crops: barley is the largest tillage crop, with wheat, oats and potatoes also grown.
Tillage is concentrated in the south and east, in Counties Wexford, Carlow, Kildare, Meath and Cork.

notes.h: Dairy and beef: exports and environmental costs
points: EU milk quotas ended on 1 April 2015, and dairy cow numbers and milk output rose strongly afterwards.
About 90% of Irish beef and dairy output is exported (Bord Bia, 2020s).
A large cattle herd brings exports, food-processing jobs and incomes to rural areas.
Agriculture is the largest single source of Ireland's greenhouse gas emissions, about 38% (EPA, 2022 data), with methane from livestock a main part of this.
Nitrate and phosphate runoff from fields pollutes rivers and lakes, and livestock release ammonia.
Kerrygold butter is exported by Ornua, the dairy co-operatives' export company; the brand was launched in 1962.
Kerry Group (headquarters Tralee, Co. Kerry) and Glanbia (headquarters Kilkenny) are major food companies.
Tayto crisps were first made in 1954 by Joe 'Spud' Murphy.
Bord Bia, the Irish food board, promotes Irish food.
Guinness is made at St James's Gate Brewery, Dublin, a site dating from 1759.
Jameson Irish whiskey is made at Midleton Distillery, Co. Cork; its producer, Irish Distillers, is owned by Pernod Ricard.
Baileys Irish Cream was launched in 1974.
Ireland has a long, indented coastline with sheltered harbours and a wide continental shelf.
Plankton-rich waters and the North Atlantic Drift support productive stocks, especially pelagic (surface-swimming) fish such as mackerel.
Six State Fishery Harbour Centres: Killybegs (Co. Donegal), Castletownbere (Co. Cork), Dingle (Co. Kerry), Rossaveel (Co. Galway), Dunmore East (Co. Waterford) and Howth (Co. Dublin).
Killybegs is Ireland's largest fishing port and lands mainly pelagic fish.
Bord Iascaigh Mhara (BIM) is the Irish sea fisheries board.

notes.h: Fishing: quotas and value to the economy
points: The EU Common Fisheries Policy (1983) sets fishing quotas for member states.
The 2020 EU–UK Brexit trade agreement reduced Irish quotas.
Mackerel is the most valuable species landed in Ireland.
Fishing earns export income, provides jobs in remote coastal communities and supports fish processing.
Forest cover is about 11% (2020s), among the lowest in the EU.
Coillte, the State forestry company, was set up in 1988; Sitka spruce is the main plantation tree.
Wood processing employs few people because the forest area is small, plantations are young, sawmills and board mills are highly mechanised, and timber is partly exported unprocessed.
Coillte's board mills are Medite, making MDF at Clonmel, Co. Tipperary, and SmartPly, making oriented strand board at Belview, Co. Kilkenny, on Waterford Port.
Tara Mines, Navan, Co. Meath, is Europe's largest zinc mine and has produced since 1977; it is owned by Boliden.
The Corrib gas field off Co. Mayo first flowed in December 2015.
ESB's peat-fired power stations at Shannonbridge (West Offaly) and Lanesborough (Lough Ree) closed in December 2020.
Bord na Móna's peat harvesting for electricity has ended.
Foreign direct investment (FDI) is investment by foreign companies that set up or expand plants and offices in Ireland.
IDA client companies, mostly foreign-owned, employ about 300,000 people (2023).
Low corporation tax, IDA grants and serviced sites attract firms to Ireland.
A young, educated, English-speaking workforce gives firms access to skilled labour.
Access to the EU single market and clusters of similar firms add to the attraction.
Ireland's time zone, between the USA and Asia, suits firms that serve both.
Cork Harbour, especially Ringaskiddy and Little Island, is one of the world's largest concentrations of pharmaceutical and chemical plants.
Pfizer, Janssen (Johnson & Johnson) and Novartis have plants at Ringaskiddy; Eli Lilly is at Kinsale, Co. Cork; Pfizer also has a site at Grange Castle, Clondalkin, Dublin.
Pharmaceuticals and chemicals are Ireland's largest goods exports, about half or more of the total (2020s).
Galway is one of Europe's leading medical-technology clusters: Boston Scientific opened there in 1994 and Medtronic is at Parkmore.
Intel at Leixlip, Co. Kildare, opened in 1989 and is Ireland's largest private-sector investment, worth billions of euro.
Fab 34 at Leixlip opened in 2023 and makes advanced chips using extreme ultraviolet (EUV) lithography.
Apple's European headquarters at Hollyhill, Cork, opened in 1980 and employs about 6,000 staff (2020s).
Enterprise Ireland, set up in 1998, supports Irish-owned firms.
Irish-founded firms that grew into multinationals include CRH (building materials) and Smurfit Kappa (paper packaging), which merged with WestRock in 2024 as Smurfit Westrock.
Ryanair, an Irish-founded airline, is a tertiary firm.
Ireland has a dual economy: a highly productive foreign-owned sector sits beside a smaller, lower-productivity Irish-owned sector.
Dependence on a few large US multinationals means that a single firm's decisions can change output and jobs.
The 15% global minimum tax for very large groups (see the Single Market, euro and corporation tax block) reduces the advantage of Ireland's low rate.
In September 2024 the EU Court of Justice ruled that Apple must pay Ireland about €13 billion plus interest in back taxes; the case had been begun by the European Commission in 2016.
US trade and tax policy changes: the USA raised tariffs on EU goods in 2025.
Brexit: the UK left the EU on 31 January 2020 and the transition ended on 31 December 2020, changing trade, supply chains and access to the UK market.
High housing and living costs make it hard to attract staff.
Electricity grid and water constraints, and high energy costs, limit expansion.
Competition from lower-cost countries.

notes.b: A footloose industry is not tied to a location by raw materials or power, so it can locate almost anywhere.
points: Footloose firms choose places with skilled labour, good communications, quality of life and government incentives.
Services such as software, internet and data processing are the most footloose.
Silicon Docks is the Grand Canal Dock area, south of the River Liffey, where digital firms cluster.
Microsoft has been in Ireland since 1985; Google has had its European headquarters in Dublin since 2003, at Barrow Street on Grand Canal Dock.
Meta (Facebook), LinkedIn and Salesforce also have large Dublin offices.
The Dublin Docklands Development Authority, set up in 1997, was created to plan and regenerate the docklands.

notes.h: Why the Dublin region clusters service firms
points: Skilled graduates come from Trinity College Dublin, UCD, DCU, TU Dublin and Maynooth University.
Firms recruit staff from across the EU for offices serving Europe.
Dublin Airport, with over 30 million passengers a year (2023), and fibre connectivity link the region to the world.
A low tax rate and government incentives attract firms.
Agglomeration: firms gain from being close to each other, sharing skills and suppliers, so one firm attracts others.

notes.h: Effects of the Dublin service cluster
points: The cluster provides high-paid jobs in offices and related services.
Demand for offices and housing has pushed rents up.
The concentration of firms and workers adds to congestion in Dublin.
Data centres used about a fifth (about 21%) of Ireland's metered electricity in 2023 (CSO), and most are in the Dublin region.
A cool climate reduces cooling costs; fibre links connect them to global networks; firms cluster near each other; and tax is favourable.
The problem is electricity demand: EirGrid stated in 2022 that it would not connect new data centres in the Dublin region until about 2028.

notes.h: Shannon Free Zone and aircraft leasing
points: Brendan O'Regan opened the world's first duty-free airport shop at Shannon in 1947.
The Shannon Free Airport Development Company (SFADCo) was set up in 1959, and the Shannon Free Zone that year offered firms tax relief and duty-free import of components.
Aircraft leasing grew from Shannon after Guinness Peat Aviation (GPA) was founded there in 1975 by Tony Ryan, who co-founded Ryanair in the 1980s.
Ireland now manages about half of the world's leased commercial aircraft (2020s, approximately).

notes.b: Silicon Valley is the original region of footloose high-technology and service industry.
points: It covers the Santa Clara Valley and the southern San Francisco Bay Area; the name comes from the silicon used in microchips.
Stanford University at Palo Alto encouraged spin-off firms and set up Stanford Research Park in 1951.
Hewlett-Packard was founded in a Palo Alto garage in 1939; Intel was founded in Santa Clara in 1968.
Apple is based in Cupertino and Google in Mountain View.
Problems: very high house prices and rents, traffic congestion, and homelessness alongside great wealth.

notes.b: Financial services are a highly footloose, high-value tertiary activity.
points: They include banking, insurance, fund administration, asset management, aircraft leasing, payments and fintech.
The International Financial Services Centre (IFSC) was set up in 1987 by the Charles Haughey government on the derelict Custom House Docks, on the north bank of the Liffey.
Approved firms paid a 10% corporation tax rate, later replaced by the 12.5% national rate.
Firms were attracted by the low tax rate, government incentives, an educated English-speaking workforce, EU access, the time zone, and the chance to regenerate a declining dock area.
The IFSC became one of the world's largest centres for investment funds; Irish-domiciled funds held over €3 trillion in assets (2020s, Central Bank of Ireland).
Aircraft leasing is a second specialism, described in the Shannon Free Zone and aircraft leasing block.
Effects: high-value jobs and the regeneration of the north docklands, served by the Luas Red Line from 2004, with new housing nearby.
The 2008 banking crisis damaged confidence in Irish finance, and the Central Bank of Ireland regulates the sector.
After the 2016 Brexit vote, Bank of America and Barclays moved their main EU operations to Dublin, an opportunity for Ireland.
The City of London (the Square Mile) was deregulated by the 'Big Bang' of the London Stock Exchange in October 1986.
Canary Wharf, built on derelict London docks from the late 1980s, became a second financial district.
After Brexit, some banks moved EU operations from London to Dublin, Frankfurt and Paris.
Physical attractions: climate, coast, scenery, mountains and lakes.
Cultural and historic attractions: heritage sites, language, music, festivals and sport.
Access: airports, ports, roads and low-cost airlines.
Accommodation and services, and marketing by government agencies.
Cost and exchange rates, and safety and political stability.
About 11 million overseas visits were made to the Republic of Ireland in 2019 (CSO).
Tourism supported about a quarter of a million jobs in 2019 (industry estimate).
Britain, the USA and continental Europe (Germany, France) are the main source markets.
Fáilte Ireland, set up in 2003, develops tourism in the Republic; Tourism Ireland, an all-island marketing body created under the Good Friday Agreement (1998), markets the island abroad.
The Wild Atlantic Way, launched in 2014, runs about 2,500 km from Inishowen to Kinsale; Ireland's Ancient East was launched in 2015.
Overseas visits collapsed in 2020–2021 during COVID-19 travel restrictions.
Job losses, closed hotels and lost revenue hit remote areas that depend on visitors.
International airports: Dublin, Shannon, Cork, Ireland West Airport Knock (opened 1986) and Kerry Airport at Farranfore.
Ferry ports: Dublin Port (to Holyhead), Rosslare Europort (to Fishguard and Pembroke, and since Brexit more direct routes to France) and Port of Cork at Ringaskiddy (to Roscoff, France).
Ryanair, Europe's largest airline by passengers (2020s), is headquartered in Swords, Co. Dublin.

notes.h: Why the east coast attracts most visitors
points: Dublin Airport and Dublin Port are the main entry points for overseas visitors.
Dublin is the capital, with the most attractions, hotels and events.
Short trips, such as city breaks, suit visitors who arrive in Dublin.
Good motorway and rail links radiate from Dublin.
The Guinness Storehouse, opened in 2000, is Ireland's most visited fee-paying attraction.
The Book of Kells is at Trinity College Dublin; Dublin Zoo is in the Phoenix Park.
Brú na Bóinne (Newgrange), Co. Meath, has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1993.
The Glendalough monastic site and Powerscourt are both in Co. Wicklow.

notes.h: Attractions on the west and north coasts
points: The Cliffs of Moher, Co. Clare, are part of the Burren and Cliffs of Moher UNESCO Global Geopark.
Kylemore Abbey is in Connemara.
The Giant's Causeway, Co. Antrim, in Northern Ireland, has been a UNESCO site since 1986.

notes.b: Co. Kerry, centred on Killarney and the Ring of Kerry, is a mass-tourism region.
points: Killarney National Park, created in 1932 from the Muckross estate, was Ireland's first national park; the estate was given to the State by the Bourn Vincent family.
Attractions include Muckross House, the Lakes of Killarney, Torc Waterfall, the Gap of Dunloe and Ross Castle.
Carrauntoohil (1,038 m), in the Macgillycuddy's Reeks, is Ireland's highest mountain.
The Ring of Kerry is a circular route of about 180 km around the Iveragh Peninsula.

Skellig Michael, an early Christian monastery on a rocky island, has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1996 and was a film location for Star Wars: The Force Awakens (2015) and The Last Jedi (2017).
The Dingle Peninsula, with the Slea Head drive and the Dingle Gaeltacht, adds to the county's attractions.
Tourism in Killarney dates from the 18th and 19th centuries.
The railway reached Killarney in 1853.
Queen Victoria visited Killarney in 1861.
Positive: jobs and income in a peripheral region, services kept open in rural areas, and heritage protected through tourism income.
Negative: seasonal jobs, with work concentrated in the summer months.
Negative: traffic and coach congestion on the narrow roads of the Ring of Kerry.
Negative: erosion on the Carrauntoohil paths and litter on popular trails.
Negative: holiday homes push up house prices and make affordable housing scarce for local workers.
Spain received about 84 million international tourists in 2019 and about 94 million in 2024, a record (INE).
Tourism provides over a tenth of Spain's GDP (2020s, approximate).
Mass tourism grew from the 1960s under the Franco regime, which promoted it with the 'Spain is different' slogan to earn foreign currency.
Causes: sun and beaches; package holidays and jet aircraft; cheap flights; low costs; and proximity to northern Europe.
Benidorm, on the Costa Blanca, was a small fishing village transformed in the 1950s and 1960s by mayor Pedro Zaragoza's plan for high-rise buildings close to the beach.
The Gran Hotel Bali (186 m, opened 2002) was then Europe's tallest hotel.
The Costa del Sol has Málaga airport, Torremolinos and Marbella.
The Balearic Islands, in the Mediterranean, include Mallorca (Palma, Magaluf) and Ibiza.
Effects: jobs, foreign earnings and infrastructure.
Problems: 'ribbon development' of concrete along the coast, and high-rise overdevelopment.
Water shortages: Catalonia declared a drought emergency in early 2024.
Low-paid seasonal jobs, and rising rents as short-term tourist lets spread.
Large anti-overtourism protests took place in 2024 in Barcelona, Mallorca and the Canary Islands.
The Balearic and Catalan governments charge tourist taxes.
Barcelona plans to end licences for about 10,000 tourist apartments by 2028.
Industrial decline is the long-term fall in the number of firms and jobs in a traditional industry or region.
Evidence: plant closures, derelict sites and buildings, high unemployment, emigration (out-migration), falling population in industrial towns, and social problems.
The end of protection and the opening to free trade exposed small, inefficient protected firms, through the Anglo-Irish Free Trade Agreement (1965) and EEC membership (1973).
Competition from low-wage countries.
Recessions, such as those of the 1980s and 2008.
New technology replacing labour.
EU policy reform, such as the reform of the EU sugar regime.
Corporate decisions to move production to lower-cost locations, as with Dell in Limerick (see the Irish examples blocks).
The Dunlop tyre factory in Cork closed in 1983.
Ford's Marina plant in Cork closed in 1984; Ford's Cork company was founded in 1917.
Verolme Cork Dockyard at Rushbrooke closed in 1984.

notes.h: Steel, sugar, crystal and computer closures, 2001 to 2009
points: Irish Steel (later Ispat) closed on Haulbowline Island, Cork Harbour, in 2001; the site needed a costly clean-up of contaminated waste.
Irish Sugar (Greencore) closed its Carlow beet factory in 2005 and its Mallow factory in 2006, ending Irish sugar production after EU sugar-regime reform.
Waterford Crystal's Kilbarry factory closed in January 2009 when the company went into receivership.
Dell opened at Raheen, Limerick, in 1990; in January 2009 it announced that manufacturing would move to Łódź, Poland, with the loss of about 1,900 jobs, while sales and service stayed in Ireland.

notes.h: Moneypoint and the end of coal
points: Moneypoint, Co. Clare, a coal-fired power station built in the 1980s, was Ireland's last coal-burning power station.
Coal burning at Moneypoint ended in 2025, part of the move away from fossil fuels that also closed the peat stations.
Unemployment reached about 17% in the mid-1980s.
Heavy emigration in the 1980s drew skilled people away from the affected towns.
Derelict docklands and empty factories were left in city and town centres.
Local towns lost skills and spending as jobs disappeared.
Replacement investment: the IDA and Enterprise Ireland sought new firms to replace lost jobs.
Regeneration of the Dublin Docklands and the IFSC (see the IFSC blocks).
Regeneration of Cork Docklands, through a city plan to redevelop the old port quays.
Heritage reuse: a smaller House of Waterford Crystal factory and visitor centre opened in Waterford city centre (the Mall) in 2010.
Retraining for displaced workers.
The EU Just Transition Fund supports the Midlands peat region.
Coalfield and steel regions of decline elsewhere in Europe are covered in the Socio-economic regions notes.

notes.b: Economic activity is unevenly spread across Ireland.
points: The Greater Dublin Area had about 2.1 million people in Census 2022, about 40% of the State's population, and holds most multinational and service jobs, along with Cork, Galway and Limerick.
The Border, Midlands and West have more small farms, fewer FDI jobs and lower incomes.
The Border, Midland and Western (BMW) region was designated for EU funding in 1999 (Objective 1 for 2000–2006); the rest of the State was the Southern and Eastern region.
The National Planning Framework (Project Ireland 2040, 2018) aims for Galway, Cork, Limerick and Waterford to each grow by at least 50% by 2040.

keyTerms.definition: Economic activity that extracts raw materials from nature, such as farming, fishing, forestry and mining.
Economic activity that processes raw materials or assembles components into goods, including construction.
Economic activity that provides services, such as banking, tourism, teaching and transport.
Farming that rears livestock, such as beef and dairy cattle, sheep and pigs.
Arable farming that grows crops, such as barley, wheat, oats and potatoes.
Investment by a foreign company that sets up or expands plants or offices in Ireland.
An economy with a highly productive foreign-owned sector beside a smaller, less productive Irish-owned sector.
An industry not tied to one location by raw materials or power, so it can locate almost anywhere.
The advantage firms gain by clustering near each other, sharing skills and suppliers.
The International Financial Services Centre, set up in Dublin in 1987 on the derelict Custom House Docks.
The long-term fall in the number of firms and jobs in a traditional industry or region.
Building in a continuous strip along a coastline or road, typical of coastal resorts.
Protest against so many visitors that local residents, housing and services are placed under pressure.

factCards.term: Ireland from protection to free trade, 1932 to 1973
factCards.definition: Protection: the Control of Manufactures Acts (1932, 1934) and high tariffs shielded Irish firms, leaving 1950s unemployment and emigration. Opening: IDA 1949; Export Profits Tax Relief 1956; Whitaker's First Programme 1958; Anglo-Irish Free Trade Agreement 1965; EEC 1973.

factCards.term: How Ireland built a skilled, open economy after 1966: four dated steps
factCards.definition: Free second-level education (announced 1966 by Donogh O'Malley, introduced 1967) built an educated workforce; the EU Single Market began in 1993; the euro came in 1999 (notes and coins 2002); corporation tax on trading profits was 12.5% from 2003.

factCards.term: Celtic Tiger, mid-1990s to 2007: causes and effects
factCards.definition: Driven first by exports and FDI, especially US technology and pharmaceutical firms, then by a property and construction boom. Unemployment fell to about 4–5% by the mid-2000s; net immigration replaced emigration, with large inflows from new EU states after 2004.

factCards.term: Irish banking crash: the sequence of events, 2007 to 2013
factCards.definition: Property bubble burst 2007–2008; bank guarantee 30 September 2008; Anglo Irish Bank nationalised January 2009; NAMA set up later in 2009 to take over property loans; EU–IMF programme of €67.5 billion in external loans agreed November 2010, exited December 2013.

factCards.term: Why the Irish government built up such a large debt after 2008
factCards.definition: The state borrowed heavily to rescue the banks (bank guarantee 2008, Anglo Irish Bank nationalised 2009, EU–IMF loans 2010) while its tax base collapsed with the property crash, so government debt peaked at about 120% of GDP in 2012.

factCards.term: Five benefits of high employment to an economy
factCards.definition: More income-tax and VAT revenue; lower welfare spending; consumer spending that supports jobs in other sectors; less emigration, so skilled people stay; more government money to invest in infrastructure and services.

factCards.term: Irish agriculture: key figures and where tillage is concentrated
factCards.definition: Census of Agriculture 2020: about 135,000 farms averaging about 33 hectares; about 7 million cattle (2020s). Mild winters and reliable rain favour grass-based livestock. Barley is the largest tillage crop; tillage is concentrated in Wexford, Carlow, Kildare, Meath and Cork.

factCards.term: Ireland's large cattle herd: benefits and environmental problems
factCards.definition: Benefits: exports (about 90% of beef and dairy output), food-processing jobs, rural incomes; dairying grew after milk quotas ended on 1 April 2015. Problems: methane makes agriculture Ireland's largest source of greenhouse gases, about 38% (EPA, 2022 data); nitrate and phosphate runoff; ammonia.

factCards.term: Name an Irish food product and an Irish drink, with their makers
factCards.definition: Food: Kerrygold butter (Ornua, launched 1962); Tayto crisps (first made 1954 by Joe 'Spud' Murphy). Drink: Guinness (brewed at St James's Gate, Dublin, since 1759); Jameson whiskey (Irish Distillers, Midleton, Co. Cork); Baileys Irish Cream (launched 1974).

factCards.term: Irish fishing: natural advantages and value to the economy
factCards.definition: Advantages: a long, indented coastline with sheltered harbours; a wide continental shelf; plankton-rich waters and the North Atlantic Drift; pelagic stocks, mackerel being the most valuable. Value: exports, jobs in remote coastal communities, fish processing.

factCards.term: Name Ireland's six State Fishery Harbour Centres
factCards.definition: Killybegs (Co. Donegal), the largest, landing mainly pelagic fish; Castletownbere (Co. Cork); Dingle (Co. Kerry); Rossaveel (Co. Galway); Dunmore East (Co. Waterford); Howth (Co. Dublin).

factCards.term: Ireland's main manufacturing sectors: a location and firm for each
factCards.definition: Pharmaceuticals and chemicals, the largest goods exports: Cork Harbour (Pfizer, Janssen, Novartis at Ringaskiddy). Medical devices: Galway (Boston Scientific 1994, Medtronic). ICT: Intel, Leixlip (1989); Apple, Cork (1980). Food and drink: Kerry Group (Tralee) and Glanbia (Kilkenny).

factCards.term: Challenges facing industry in Ireland: name seven
factCards.definition: Dependence on a few US multinationals; the 15% minimum tax for very large groups (2024); US tariffs on EU goods (2025); Brexit; housing costs that deter staff; grid and water limits (EirGrid will not connect new Dublin data centres until about 2028); lower-cost rivals.

factCards.term: Silicon Docks, Dublin: where it is, named firms and effects
factCards.definition: Grand Canal Dock, south of the Liffey. Google has had its European headquarters in Dublin since 2003, now on Barrow Street; Meta and LinkedIn also have large offices in the area. Effects: high-paid jobs, rising rents, congestion.

factCards.term: Why service and footloose firms cluster in the Dublin region
factCards.definition: Graduates from Trinity College Dublin, UCD, DCU, TU Dublin and Maynooth University; EU-wide recruitment; Dublin Airport (over 30 million passengers, 2023) and fibre links; low tax and incentives; agglomeration, as firms share skills and suppliers.

factCards.term: Shannon: duty-free shop, Free Zone and aircraft leasing
factCards.definition: Brendan O'Regan opened the world's first duty-free airport shop at Shannon in 1947; the Shannon Free Zone (1959) gave firms tax relief and duty-free imports. Tony Ryan founded GPA at Shannon in 1975; Ireland now manages about half the world's leased aircraft.

factCards.term: Silicon Valley, California: origins, named firms and problems
factCards.definition: Stanford University encouraged spin-off firms and opened its Research Park in 1951; Hewlett-Packard began in a Palo Alto garage in 1939; Intel (founded 1968) is headquartered in Santa Clara; Apple is at Cupertino, Google at Mountain View. Problems: high house prices, congestion, homelessness.

factCards.term: IFSC, Dublin: when, where and why it was set up
factCards.definition: Set up in 1987 by the Charles Haughey government on the derelict Custom House Docks, north of the Liffey. Reasons: a 10% tax rate for approved firms, government incentives, an educated English-speaking workforce, EU access, the time zone, and regeneration of the docks.

factCards.term: IFSC: growth, effects and the Brexit opportunity
factCards.definition: Irish-domiciled funds hold over €3 trillion (2020s). Effects: high-value jobs; regeneration of the north docklands, served by the Luas Red Line (2004). After the 2016 Brexit vote, Bank of America and Barclays moved their main EU operations to Dublin.

factCards.term: Factors that influence the development of tourism in an area
factCards.definition: Physical attractions (climate, coast, scenery); cultural and historic attractions (heritage, music, festivals, sport); access (airports, ports, low-cost airlines); accommodation and services; marketing; cost and exchange rates; safety and political stability.

factCards.term: Irish tourism: its importance and the COVID-19 collapse
factCards.definition: About 11 million overseas visits and about a quarter of a million jobs (2019); main markets Britain, the USA, Germany and France. COVID-19 travel restrictions collapsed visits in 2020–2021, causing job losses, closed hotels and lost revenue in remote areas.

factCards.term: Irish tourism agencies and marketing brands
factCards.definition: Fáilte Ireland (2003) develops tourism in the Republic; Tourism Ireland, created under the Good Friday Agreement (1998), markets the whole island. The Wild Atlantic Way (2014) runs about 2,500 km from Inishowen to Kinsale; Ireland's Ancient East followed in 2015.

factCards.term: Why Ireland's east coast attracts the most visitors
factCards.definition: Dublin Airport and Dublin Port are the main entry points; Dublin, the capital, has the most attractions, hotels and events; city breaks suit short trips; good motorway and rail links radiate from Dublin.

factCards.term: Irish tourist attractions: four in the east and two in the west
factCards.definition: East: the Guinness Storehouse (2000), the most visited fee-paying attraction; the Book of Kells, Trinity College Dublin; Brú na Bóinne (Newgrange), UNESCO 1993; Glendalough, Co. Wicklow. West: the Cliffs of Moher, Co. Clare; Kylemore Abbey, Connemara.

factCards.term: Co. Kerry as a mass-tourism region: main attractions
factCards.definition: Killarney National Park (1932), Ireland's first, from the Muckross estate; the Lakes of Killarney, Torc Waterfall, Gap of Dunloe; Carrauntoohil (1,038 m), Ireland's highest mountain; the Ring of Kerry (about 180 km); Skellig Michael (UNESCO 1996).

factCards.term: Co. Kerry tourism: positive and negative impacts
factCards.definition: Positive: jobs and income in a peripheral region; rural services kept open; heritage protected. Negative: seasonal jobs; coach congestion on the narrow Ring of Kerry roads; erosion on Carrauntoohil paths and litter; holiday homes raising house prices for locals.

factCards.term: Spain's mass tourism: causes of its growth
factCards.definition: From the 1960s the Franco regime promoted tourism ('Spain is different') to earn foreign currency; jet aircraft and package holidays, later cheap flights; sun and beaches; low costs; nearness to northern Europe. About 84 million tourists in 2019; about 94 million in 2024.

factCards.term: Benidorm and other mass-tourism resorts in Spain
factCards.definition: Benidorm, Costa Blanca: a fishing village transformed in the 1950s–60s by mayor Pedro Zaragoza's high-rise plan; the Gran Hotel Bali (186 m, 2002) was then Europe's tallest hotel. Costa del Sol: Torremolinos, Marbella. Balearics: Mallorca (Magaluf), Ibiza.

factCards.term: Spain's mass tourism: four problems
factCards.definition: Concrete ribbon development and high-rise overbuilding on coasts; water shortages (Catalonia's drought emergency, early 2024); low-paid seasonal jobs; rents raised by short-term tourist lets, prompting 2024 protests in Barcelona, Mallorca and the Canary Islands.

factCards.term: Spain's mass tourism: economic effects and two responses
factCards.definition: Effects: jobs, foreign earnings and infrastructure; tourism gives over a tenth of Spain's GDP (2020s). Responses: the Balearic and Catalan governments charge tourist taxes; Barcelona plans to end licences for about 10,000 tourist apartments by 2028.

factCards.term: Evidence of industrial decline in a region: give six types
factCards.definition: Plant closures; derelict sites and buildings; high unemployment; emigration or out-migration; falling population in industrial towns; social problems.

factCards.term: Causes of industrial decline in Ireland
factCards.definition: The end of protection exposed small, inefficient firms (Anglo-Irish Free Trade Agreement 1965, EEC 1973); competition from low-wage countries; recessions (1980s, 2008); new technology replacing labour; EU reform such as the sugar regime; firms moving production abroad.

factCards.term: Cork's 1980s closures and the effects of decline
factCards.definition: Dunlop's tyre factory closed in 1983; Ford's Marina plant and Verolme Cork Dockyard, Rushbrooke, closed in 1984. Effects: job losses in Cork as national unemployment reached about 17% in the mid-1980s; heavy emigration; derelict docklands; lost skills and spending in local towns.

factCards.term: Irish industrial closures since 2001: name five with dates
factCards.definition: Irish Steel, Haulbowline (2001), leaving a contaminated site; Irish Sugar's Carlow (2005) and Mallow (2006) factories after EU sugar reform; Waterford Crystal, Kilbarry (January 2009); Dell manufacturing, Limerick (2009, about 1,900 jobs); peat power stations (2020).

factCards.term: Responses to industrial decline in Ireland
factCards.definition: IDA and Enterprise Ireland replacement investment; regeneration of the Dublin Docklands (Docklands Development Authority 1997, IFSC 1987) and Cork Docklands; heritage reuse, like the House of Waterford Crystal on the Mall (2010); retraining; the EU Just Transition Fund.

questions.prompt: Describe and explain the development of financial services in a developed economy you have studied.
questions.model: 1) Origin: the International Financial Services Centre (IFSC) was set up in Dublin in 1987. 2) Site: it was built on the derelict Custom House Docks, on the north bank of the Liffey, a declining dock area. 3) Government: the Charles Haughey government created the IFSC and gave it incentives. 4) Tax: approved firms paid a 10% corporation tax rate, later replaced by the 12.5% national rate. 5) Workforce: an educated, English-speaking workforce attracted firms. 6) EU access: a base inside the EU single market suited banks and funds serving Europe. 7) Time zone: Dublin's time zone suited firms working with other financial centres. 8) Growth: the IFSC became one of the world's largest centres for investment funds, with Irish-domiciled funds holding over €3 trillion in assets (2020s). 9) Aircraft leasing: the leasing business grew from Shannon after Guinness Peat Aviation was founded there in 1975, and Ireland now manages about half of the world's leased commercial aircraft (approximately). 10) Effects: high-value jobs and regeneration of the north docklands, with the Luas Red Line (2004) serving the IFSC and new housing nearby. 11) Brexit: after the 2016 Brexit vote, Bank of America and Barclays moved their main EU operations to Dublin. 12) Risk: the 2008 banking crisis left Anglo Irish Bank nationalised in January 2009 and led to NAMA being set up in 2009 to take over property loans. 13) Reputation: financial services depend on trust, and the Central Bank of Ireland regulates the sector.

questions.prompt: Examine the evidence of industrial decline in a developed economy you have studied.
questions.model: 1) Definition: industrial decline is the long-term fall in the number of firms and jobs in a traditional industry or region. 2) Evidence: plant closures, derelict sites, high unemployment, emigration and falling population in industrial towns. 3) Cause: the end of protection and the opening to free trade, through the Anglo-Irish Free Trade Agreement (1965) and EEC membership (1973), exposed small, inefficient firms. 4) Cause: competition from low-wage countries. 5) Cause: recessions in the 1980s and 2008. 6) Cause: new technology replacing labour. 7) Cause: corporate decisions to move production abroad. 8) Example: the Dunlop tyre factory (1983), Ford's Marina plant (1984) and Verolme Cork Dockyard (1984) closed in Cork. 9) Example: Irish Steel on Haulbowline Island, Cork Harbour, closed in 2001. 10) Example: Irish Sugar closed its Carlow factory in 2005 and its Mallow factory in 2006 after EU sugar-regime reform. 11) Example: Waterford Crystal's Kilbarry factory closed in January 2009. 12) Example: Dell in Limerick announced in 2009 that manufacturing would move to Poland, with about 1,900 jobs lost. 13) Example: the ESB's peat-fired power stations closed in December 2020. 14) Effects: unemployment of about 17% in the mid-1980s, heavy emigration and derelict docklands. 15) Responses: replacement investment by the IDA and Enterprise Ireland, regeneration of the Dublin and Cork docklands, the House of Waterford Crystal visitor centre, retraining, and the EU Just Transition Fund for the Midlands.

questions.prompt: (i) Name one tertiary activity in a developed economy you have studied. (ii) Explain the advantages this economy has for it. (iii) Describe one challenge it faces.
questions.model: (i) Tourism in Ireland. (ii) 1) Physical attractions: scenery, coast, mountains and lakes, such as the Ring of Kerry and Carrauntoohil in Co. Kerry. 2) Heritage: Brú na Bóinne (Newgrange), a UNESCO site since 1993; Skellig Michael, a UNESCO site since 1996; and the Book of Kells in Dublin. 3) Access: Dublin Airport, Shannon, Cork and Kerry airports, Dublin Port and Rosslare Europort, and low-cost airlines such as Ryanair. 4) Marketing: Tourism Ireland promotes the island abroad, with the Wild Atlantic Way and Ireland's Ancient East as brands. 5) Language: English is widely spoken, which suits visitors from Britain and the USA. 6) Income: tourism brings in overseas earnings and supported about a quarter of a million jobs in 2019. (iii) Challenge: seasonality. 1) Tourism is concentrated in the summer months, so many jobs are seasonal and workers are employed for only part of the year. 2) Busy months bring congestion on roads such as the Ring of Kerry. 3) In quiet months, hotels and attractions are underused, which lowers their income.
